accuracy.reason: Live MySQL 8.4 documentation supports engine scope, SQL-mode example, snapshot/current-read distinction, clustered/secondary lookup, asynchronous lag and backup-plus-log recovery. Guarantees are qualified by settings and failure conditions; diagrams preserve these distinctions.

evidence.quote: Receipt and application are different stages; reads can remain old until application catches up.
Delayed flushing can lose recent commits; lost storage still needs another durable copy or backup.

mechanisms.reason: All nine cards teach their objectives across the connected stack. Learner can trace SQL through engine/storage, protected check/change, aborted-transaction retry, secondary-to-clustered lookup, replication receipt/application and historical replay. The locking-read alternative satisfies scarce-unit protection without requiring an additional conditional-update tutorial.

evidence.quote: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads and locks records inside a transaction. Check and change the protected value before committing; an earlier unprotected check does not reserve it.
Stores indexed columns plus the primary-key values used to find the complete row.

coherence.reason: Server and engine scope precede rules and transactions; isolation explains concurrent effects, indexes connect lookup to write costs, then replication and recovery feed the final choice. Later cards elaborate earlier terms without leaving a required prerequisite missing. Selective examples support distinctions without requiring a recurring story.

evidence.quote: Indexes add write work; read replicas can lag; distributing writes requires additional design. These costs follow from the mechanisms covered in this deck.

decisions.reason: Benefits are paired with resource, index, contention, freshness and recovery costs. Final selection asks for workload/failure requirements and measured restoration rather than an automatic scaling or lossless-failover promise.

evidence.quote: Clarify read/write traffic, stale-read tolerance, acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime. Bound connection demand and transaction length, then validate recovery targets; different deployment needs may favor another database.

clarity.reason: SQL-mode conversion, price snapshot and email-index examples are useful and selective. Slides 3–5 are dense and terms such as invariants/current-data rules could use plainer phrasing, but the surrounding explanations and learner transfer establish sufficiency. Shared renderer/CSS presents the supplied teaching content.

evidence.quote: For example, your transaction reads a price of 10. Another transaction changes it to 12 and commits. A second plain SELECT in your transaction still sees 10, unless your transaction also changed that row.

outcomes.reason: Learner covers separate client/server SQL, related tables/joins and shared access; schema, query, transaction and recovery design responsibilities are supported across later cards. It correctly defines engine scope, InnoDB features, actual-engine checks and remaining lock contention.

Learner supports types, unique non-null primary key, UNIQUE/NULL, required nonnegative CHECK and valid references, deployed SQL-mode/version checks and workflow limits. Explicit grouping versus autocommit, all ACID meanings, configured redo durability/storage-loss limits and external-side-effect boundary are taught and correctly applied.

Learner explains versions, first consistent-read snapshot and own changes, current locking reads, safe lock/check/decrement including no allocation when insufficient, deadlock whole-transaction retry and short locks. It also supports clustered/secondary lookup, primary-key width/stability tradeoffs, measured plans, scans and write/storage costs; stability follows from keys repeated in maintained index entries.

Learner traces source log, receipt and application, stale reads, asynchronous confirmed-write loss, freshness routing and safe promotion. It distinguishes crash recovery/failover/history, accidental-delete propagation, compatible backup plus continuous retained logs and tested recovery time/usability.

Learner integrates schema/engine selection, transaction concurrency and retry, index costs/plans, replica freshness and source-write limits, bounded connections/transactions and tested recovery requirements. Earlier replication answer supplies safe-promotion details; final answer remains conditional on workload and loss/downtime needs.

sourceChecks.claim: Confirmed SQL server/client and relational-table model in What is MySQL; the process/storage diagram represents the conventional server deployment taught here.
Confirmed InnoDB default, transaction/rollback/crash recovery, row locks and foreign keys; storage-engine distinction avoids generalizing to all tables.
Confirmed strict-mode abc-to-INT rejection versus non-strict conversion to 0/warning. CHECK Constraints followup confirms FALSE rejection versus UNKNOWN acceptance, supporting NOT NULL combination.

Confirmed default autocommit and START TRANSACTION/COMMIT/ROLLBACK grouping; innodb-parameters.html confirms default redo flush at commit and relaxed-setting loss risk. External HTTP actions are outside the described database rollback scope.

Confirmed Repeatable Read first consistent-read snapshot and separate locking behavior. innodb-locking-reads.html and innodb-deadlocks-handling.html verify lock-before-check, lock release, deadlock transaction retry and short duration.

Confirmed clustered row storage and primary keys repeated in secondary entries, including size costs. mysql-indexes.html confirms scan alternatives; deadlock handling docs confirm well-chosen indexes can reduce locked records and EXPLAIN aids selection.

Confirmed default asynchronous replication. replication-threads.html verifies separate receiver and applier stages; replication-solutions-switch.html confirms deliberate promotion and client rerouting. Loss before a surviving copy obtains an acknowledged write follows from asynchronous acknowledgement.

Confirmed PITR begins after restoring a backup; point-in-time-recovery-binlog.html verifies subsequent binlog events and selectable event positions/times. Replay includes destructive changes unless stopped appropriately; retained continuous history and restore testing bound recovery claims.

Confirmed shared transactional storage benefits from InnoDB introduction; checked isolation/index/replication/recovery pages substantiate listed costs. Requirements-led sizing and recovery testing are recommendations, not promised outcomes.
